entries.title: Chris Van Hollen Is Challenging Chuck Schumer for Democratic Leader
entries.summary: The Maryland Democrat has been critical of Schumer, who has led the caucus for nearly a decade.
entries.content:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he would challenge Chuck Schumer for the top Democratic leadership role in the Senate, arguing the party needs to take a more populist direction.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, said in a statement obtained by The Washington Sun.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” he added. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Van Hollen, a favorite among progressives who is also considering a run for president, has been critical of Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, accusing them of siding with the cryptocurrency industry and American Israel Public Affairs Committee against progressive candidates.

Schumer said earlier this week that he is confident he already has more than enough support to be reelected leader.

“I am going to be elected leader, OK, and we’re united on the issues. We’re united,” Schumer told The Sun.

Schumer has faced sharp intraparty criticism over his past handling of government funding fights, with many Democratic voters blaming the longtime lawmaker for not doing more to stand up to President Donald Trump during his second term. Nearly all of the nine newly elected Senate Democrats set to take office in January have said they would not support him as leader, and several sitting Democratic senators have also called for new leadership.

Nevertheless, Schumer again expressed confidence that he will remain Democratic leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer said in a statement issued by his office on Thursday. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together - 55 seats and counting is an amazing result- and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

On MS NOW on Thursday, Van Hollen said that he is running for leader because the midterm elections were a call to reform the political system more broadly and were not just a rejection of Trump.

“It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that's rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people, and is fueled by a corrupt political system,” Van Hollen said. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

Van Hollen said that he would tackle the first 100 days of a Democratic-led Congress differently from Schumer. Though he agreed with Schumer’s plans to reverse cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Van Hollen said that Democrats should expand their sights to reining in artificial intelligence and passing a higher federal minimum wage. 

He added that he would not have gotten involved in Democratic primaries as leader, after Schumer backed candidates in Maine and Michigan who ultimately failed to secure the party’s nomination. Van Hollen said more than 15 Senate Democrats have already pledged to support his bid for leader. 

“We should be focused on defeating Republicans, not getting involved,” Van Hollen said on MS NOW. “We have two senators right now in the United States Senate who wouldn't be there if the current majority leader had his way. He supported establishment candidates in the primaries.”

Van Hollen also called on Democrats to reject donations from AIPAC. Schumer has faced criticism from the Democratic base for accepting donations from the group. 

“Some of the richest, most powerful people in the world are spending gobs of money in these elections to try to buy a Congress that will do their bidding,” Van Hollen said. “We need to get rid of super PACs. We need to get rid of secret money. We need to get rid of the Elon Musk loophole that allows him to try to buy a Congress while getting billions of dollars in federal contracts.”

The Democratic leadership elections aren’t expected to take place until early December, however, ensuring debate over the leadership race will drag on for several more weeks.

entries.title: The Commanders Keep Hope Alive With a Win Against the Giants
entries.summary: Stefon Diggs' late touchdown lifted Washington to a 24-21 victory in a "must-win" game.
entries.content:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Last week, in the moments after another frustrating loss, Jayden Daniels didn't hesitate in calling his team's Week 10 matchup with the Giants a "must-win." On Thursday night, the Commanders quarterback helped deliver that win as Washington squeaked out a 24-21 victory on the road.

After throwing two late interceptions — his first of the year — Daniels found a way to keep the Commanders' hopes for the season alive. Given one final offensive possession, he found receiver Stefon Diggs for a 32-yard touchdown with less than a minute remaining.

"When you get the opportunity to go win the game, you just take a deep breathe and go out there and capitalize on the moment," Daniels said.

The quarterback finished with 249 yards passing and three touchdowns as the Commanders moved to 3-5-1. They now sit just two games behind New York in the NFC East standings.

"We needed that," coach Dan Quinn said after the game. "We needed every bit of it, and I had a sense it would come down to the end."

The final drive came after linebacker Sonny Styles made a key tackle for loss on Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy on a third-and-3 with just under two minutes left. At that point in the night, after Daniels threw backbreaking interceptions on consecutive fourth-quarter possessions, it appeared Washington was headed for another deflating defeat.

"If you just be the player you are, the moment can never be too big," Styles said of the defensive stop. "I think everyone understood in that moment that we needed to get a stop right there."

After forcing the punt, Washington got the ball back with 1:49 remaining. Needing to go 71 yards for a touchdown, Daniels immediately threw a bomb to Treylon Burks, who drew a defensive pass interference for 33. Suddenly in business, a Washington offense that had struggled all night perked up. Daniels hit Diggs over the middle a few plays later, and the veteran wideout broke a tackle and slipped into the open field. Without no more defenders in sight, he waltzed into the end zone.

"[Daniels is] baby Kobe," Diggs said of his quarterback. "He does not flinch. He's going to be the same player at the beginning of the game as he is at the end of the game. Things are going to happen, good and bad — he is not going to change."

The Giants, needing a field goal to tie, mounted a drive of their own but it ended with Commanders corner Rasul Douglas intercepting a jump ball on third-and-long.

"I always think I'm going to make the play," Douglas said. "When the ball is in the air, I don't ever really see the receiver. I just know I'm going to get it. ... Some guys play the man — that's not me. I want interceptions, I want the ball."

It was not the prettiest of victories for Washington. Overall, the offense still looked stagnant, punting on four of its first seven drives. The defense was up and down, limiting New York to seven points in the first half but giving up big plays in key moments. Early in the fourth quarter, the Giants took a 21-17 lead on a 66-yard touchdown by tight end Isaiah Likely. Styles and K’Lavon Chaisson ran into each other in coverage, allowing Likely to break free and sprint to the end zone.

But Washington didn't quit on the game, and the team will head back to D.C. with a key win in hand. The Commanders welcome the surging Bengals to Northwest Stadium for "Monday Night Football" on Nov. 23.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: A Tragedy in Logan Circle
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Nov. 12, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A firsthand account of the lead-up to a shooting that left one dead and shook a vibrant D.C. neighborhood. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 3/10. Gray, gusty and suddenly November. After weeks of warmth, it’s time to bundle up. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

Late last year, Matt Lambert reached out to The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler with a story pitch: his million-dollar Logan Circle penthouse had been rendered unlivable.

In a firsthand account, Brice-Saddler — who worked for The Washington Post at the time — recalls visiting Lambert at his home and listening to the doctor describe how a dispute over severe water leaks and black mold had turned into “psychological warfare” between himself, building manager James Stuart, the management company EJF Real Estate Services and their insurance defense attorneys.

“It’s affected every part of my life — my sleep, dietary habits,” Lambert said. “I pride myself on my resilience, and I’ve been kind of surprised at how much it has been affected.”

On Thursday morning, the dispute came to a violent end when Lambert killed Stuart and shot four others at and near VIDA Fitness Gym on his condo building’s ground floor.

The Sun’s Metro team reports that police were on scene within 30 seconds of receiving the first report of the shooting, which came in just before 8 a.m. After tending to victims and evacuating the building, they found Lambert in his seventh-floor penthouse and spoke with him for about an hour, during which time he fired at officers at least twice through the door. Police forced their way into the apartment after hearing a gunshot inside and found Lambert dead with a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

According to an online profile, Stuart, 46, had worked for EJF for more than a decade.

“We’re devastated,” Mayor Muriel Bowser said at a press conference. “Someone was killed in our city this morning. A senseless act of gun violence.”

The streets of Logan Circle, a vibrant neighborhood that has long served as a social hub and the home base of the District’s LGBTQ+ community, went eerily silent in the aftermath of the shooting. By Thursday afternoon, police confirmed that much of the conversation between Lambert and police centered on his dispute over building conditions. In addition to three firearms — a shotgun, a rifle and a handgun — police found containers of gasoline and other flammable materials inside his apartment.

Four victims were taken to local hospitals. Three of them have non-life-threatening injuries, and the fourth remained in critical condition Thursday.

On Thursday evening, Joel Braithwaite, who represented Lambert in the litigation, said his client had been in high spirits in the days prior to the shooting, having started a new job.

“Dr. Matt Lambert was an emergency room physician, someone that was in the business of healing people,” he said. “Litigation wears on you, and it takes a toll on people, and some of the tolls are not necessarily visible.”

At one point during a tour of his apartment last year, Lambert pointed to a copy of Sun Tzu’s “The Art of War” sitting in his stripped-down unit.

“I go through every emotion every day on this,” he told Michael. “Do I keep fighting? Do I not fight? And ‘The Art of War’ talks about, you know, the battle’s won before it’s ever fought. It says if you’re going to commit, don’t half commit, fully commit.”
Shooting Vida 15th st nw 003 (4032x3024, AR: 1.33)





FROM THE DISTRICT

A Way-no, for now. D.C.’s transportation committee has voted down a bill that would have legalized passenger service in self-driving cars operated by Waymo and other companies, stalling a nearly 15-year effort to bring this technology to the District, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. Though the legislation is dead for now, Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George told The Sun that she is pro-AV and is committed to convening agencies to take up the issue again when she is in office.

D.C. Council chambers were packed Thursday for a hearing on what At-Large council member Elissa Silverman called the District’s “house on fire”: truancy. Nearly 40% of D.C. public school students were identified aschronically absent last year, with family obligations, safety concerns and mental health challenges cited as potential causes. The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports that witnesses praised some current mitigation strategies, including the District’spilot truancy-reduction program, but agreed that more needs to be done.

One student who walks his younger sister to school said he often faces an “impossible” decision: “wait for a delayed bus, or complete a 20-minute walk to get her to school, just to still risk being marked absent or tardy.”

The staff of Washingtonian magazine has unanimously voted to authorize a one-day strike after five years of contract negotiations with management. Staffers say it’s a “last resort” needed to “cross the finish line,” The Sun’s Nicole Belcastro reports.





SPORTS

Commanders 24, Giants 21. In a game that Jayden Daniels labeled a “must-win,” the Commanders delivered. Stefon Diggs’ caught a 32-yard touchdown with less than a minute remaining and the Commanders kept hope alive with a much-needed divisional win. Daniels finished with 249 yards passing, three touchdowns and two interceptions as Washington moved to 3-5-1. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson breaks down the players and the plays that delivered a victory.

It will be a busy Saturday afternoon at Audi Field this weekend, as the much-discussed scheduling conflict between the Spirit’s NWSL semifinal and the Division III Secretaries’ Cup football game was resolved Thursday in surprising fashion. The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports that the soccer game will begin at noon, as planned, and the football game will kick off at 4:30 p.m. To pull off the tight doubleheader, stadium officials plan to paint the field with NWSL lines in yellow and NCAA yard lines in white.

There’s a lot to be excited about at Capitol One Arena this year: The revamped Wizards are looking to level up and Alex Ovechkin is savoring a farewell tour. But The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports that fans on social media have focused at least some of their attention away from the action, to where new luxury seats have proved to be an eyesore at games.

The Lexus Vault seats, connected to high-end suites that the stadium opened last year, have consistently sat empty as patrons enjoy other amenities away from the court or ice. “It became a conversation … just because of how glaringly empty they were,” one fan said. “It looks like there’s a giant empty section.”
